tip: For a real future condition, Welsh uses the future after ‘os’: ‘os bydd y bws yn hwyr’ (if the bus is late).
‘yn’ meaning 'in' becomes ‘ym’ before m: ‘ym mis Mawrth’ (in March).
‘a’ introduces an indirect yes-or-no question ('whether'): ‘a allen nhw fynd’ (whether they could go).
Adjectives soften after a feminine singular noun: ‘gwych’ becomes ‘wych’ in ‘ffordd wych’ (a wonderful way).
Add ‘-af’ for the superlative: ‘rhad’ (cheap) becomes ‘rhataf’ (cheapest), as in ‘opsiwn rhataf’.
Welsh has no verb 'to have'; ‘mae gen i’ means 'is with me': ‘mae gen i gefnder’ (I have a cousin).
‘wrth’ before a verb means 'while doing it': ‘wrth fyfyrio’ (while meditating).
‘ei’ meaning 'it' softens the next word: ‘mwynhau’ becomes ‘fwynhau’ in ‘ei fwynhau’ (enjoy it).
Use ‘mai’ for 'that' when the that-clause leads with a noun for emphasis: ‘mai'r tywydd sy'n broblem’ (that it's the weather that's the problem).
‘effeithio’ takes ‘ar’ for 'affect': ‘effeithio ar bawb’ (affect everyone); the ‘ar’ is required.
‘cyn gynted ag’ is the set phrase for 'as soon as': ‘cyn gynted ag y cyrhaeddais i’ (as soon as I arrived).
'That' follows the noun in Welsh: ‘y llyfr yna’ = that book, with ‘yna’ after what it points to.
‘pe bai’ is 'if' for imagined, unreal situations: ‘pe bai hi'n siarad Cymraeg’ (if she spoke Welsh, but she doesn't).
Welsh forms the passive with ‘cael’ plus ‘eu’ (their): ‘cael eu cyhoeddi’ means 'get their announcing' = be announced.
‘o flaen’ is a two-word position phrase, 'in front of': ‘o flaen y tŷ mae coeden fawr’ (in front of the house is a tree).
‘dod yn’ means 'become' and softens the next word: ‘meddyg’ becomes ‘feddyg’ in ‘dod yn feddyg’.
‘dylid’ means one should or it should be done, with no subject named: ‘dylid gwarchod’ = should be protected.
The word ‘o’ (of) softens the next noun: ‘bwyd’ becomes ‘fwyd’ in ‘digon o fwyd’ (plenty of food).
Us wraps the verb as ‘ein ... ni’: ‘ein gyrru ni’ = drive us. The pronoun frames the verb on both sides.
To take someone you say ‘mynd â’, literally go with: ‘mynd â'r plant’ = take the children.
The word ‘â’ changes the next word's start, p to ph: ‘pobl’ becomes ‘phobl’ in ‘dod â phobl’ (bring people).
Your (informal) frames the verb as ‘dy ... di’: ‘dy helpu di’ = help you. Formal or plural uses ‘eich ... chi’ instead.
After a number Welsh keeps the noun singular: ‘chwe mis’ = six months (month), never a plural.
‘meddai’ means said or says and reports speech, placed after the quote: ‘meddai'r meddyg’ = the doctor says.
For a future if, Welsh uses ‘bydd’ after ‘os’, not the present: ‘os bydd y trên yn llawn’ = if the train is full.
‘pan’ (when) softens the verb: ‘cyrhaedda’ becomes ‘gyrhaedda’ in ‘pan gyrhaedda i’ (when I arrive).
His shortens to ‘'i’ and softens the next word: ‘prawf’ becomes ‘brawf’ in ‘pasio'i brawf’ (pass his test).
For unreal or hypothetical ifs use ‘pe’ with ‘bawn’, not ‘os’: ‘pe bawn i'n gwybod’ = if I had known.
To report that something is, use ‘fod’: ‘dywedodd rhywun fod y bws yn hwyr’ = someone said the bus was late.
To say on a day, soften ‘dydd’ to ‘ddydd’: ‘ddydd Mercher’ = on Wednesday.
